$comment: Open Geographies canonical Elasticsearch mapping — the index-layer half of the schema (v0.1.0-draft). One mapping serves every atlas: fixed envelope + promoted fields are explicit properties; per-atlas relationships land under their relationship UUID (handled by the related_records dynamic template); per-atlas scalar UDFs land under their field UUID with *_facet companions (handled by facets_as_keyword). Every query is filtered server-side on project_id + visibility — documents from internal-intent fields are never written to this index at all.
settings_comment: searchkick_search/searchkick_search2 (below, under settings.analysis.analyzer) duplicate og_text rather than aliasing it: passing a custom `settings:` to searchkick() (see V1::Searchable.searchable_index) replaces Searchkick's own generated settings entirely instead of merging with them, but Searchkick's query builder still hardcodes those two analyzer names for any non-'*' search term (searchkick/query.rb) - without them here, a real text query 400s with 'analyzer [searchkick_search] not found'. Keep all three in sync if og_text's tokenizer/filters ever change. (Not `$comment` here - unlike the mappings section, `settings` is sent to Elasticsearch's index-settings API near-verbatim, which rejects unknown setting keys outright.)
mappings_comment: The `analyzed` multi-field on name/names/description/short_description/address exists only for Searchkick's own query DSL: a `q` full-text search goes through Searchkick's `.search(term, fields: [...])`, and its query builder always targets `<field>.analyzed` for a plain (non-exact, non-phrase) field, never the bare field itself - see searchkick/query.rb#set_fields. A raw ES client can and should still just query the bare field directly (its own analyzer is already og_text); `.analyzed` duplicates that only so Searchkick's generated query has something to hit. (Also not `$comment` inside mappings.properties itself, for the same reason `settings_comment` above isn't `$comment` inside settings - every key under `properties` is a field name, and Elasticsearch rejects a field definition that isn't a mapping object.)
slugs_comment: Every `slug` here has a `slugs` sibling on purpose - base_search_data/summarize (Searchable) always emit both together (slugs is the alternate-URL array; slug is just slugs.first, in effect), but until this fix only `slug` had an explicit property here. `slugs` fell through to the strings_as_text dynamic template (match_mapping_type: string -> analyzed text), so a `where: { slugs: 'some-slug' }` term filter - the exact thing PlacesController#show uses to look a record up by slug - silently matched nothing for a value that's really there, on every record at every nesting level, not just Places. Found live: a real Place's own `.search(where: { slugs: '...' })` returned no hit even though `.base_search_data` computed the right value.
stops_comment: stops (below) was declared with `position`/`location` before this fix - fields the generic Searchable engine never actually wrote (no per-model override backs the Tours/Instance class; it's promoted purely through the same #related mechanism as everything else). Renamed to what's really produced: `order` (the Relationship join row's own order column, threaded through generically now - see #with_relationship_order in searchable.rb) and `geo.point` (the same geo_point shape every other Place-derived summary carries, from #extras, not a Tour-specific `location` field). This is the same class of drift already fixed once for `slugs` above - a declared shape nothing actually produces isn't a mapping conflict ES rejects outright (dynamic mapping just silently adds whatever fields the real document does have alongside the declared-but-unpopulated ones), so it doesn't surface as an error, only as a client-facing gap: `order`/`geo` would just be silently missing from every stop.
order_comment: `order` (media/works/people/places/map_layers/stops, below) is genuinely optional, not just nullable - it's the Relationship join row's own order column, and most relationships across every atlas were never curator-ordered (nothing before this made ordering a first-class expectation, so the column defaults to nil for most existing rows). #with_relationship_order (searchable.rb) omits the key entirely rather than writing `order: null` when there's no real value - a client should check for the key's presence, not assume it and get null. Items ARE already returned pre-sorted by it (#related's own `.order(:order)` query, Postgres' NULLS LAST default putting unordered items after ordered ones) - `order` on each item is there so a client that filters/merges/re-sorts client-side can still recover the intended order afterward, not so the client has to sort it itself in the common case.
